hook.line: Tomás has asked Vale to run the café with him, fifty-fifty. She's in, on conditions, and every condition is something she wants *him* to do. English says I want you to. Spanish needs one small word and a new ending.
hook.es: Quiero que lo pongas en un papel.
hook.en: I want you to put it on paper. (to a friend)

examples.en: I want you to work with me. (to a friend)

examples.es: Necesito que me ayudes con la cocina.
examples.en: I need you to help me with the kitchen. (to a friend)
Do you want me to call you tomorrow? (to a friend)

examples.es: No quiero que hables con Altamira.
examples.en: I don't want you to talk to Altamira. (to a friend)

examples.es: Hernando no quiere que griten delante de los clientes.
examples.en: Hernando doesn't want them to shout in front of the customers.
I need you to come early. (to a friend)
I want to work with you. (to a friend)

rule:
English says I want you to come. Spanish can't build it that way. It says I want that you come: *Quiero que vengas.*

Two pieces: *que*, then the verb in a new shape. You already know that shape. It's the *usted* command, with the usual ending for the person:

*hable*: *que hables*, *que hable*, *que hablemos*, *que hablen*
*coma*: *que comas*, *que coma*, *que comamos*, *que coman*
*venga*: *que vengas*, *que venga*, *que vengamos*, *que vengan*

*-ar* verbs get an *e*, *-er* and *-ir* verbs get an *a*: the opposite vowel. For I, it's the same as for he or she: *¿Quieres que te llame?*

The test is one question: is it the same person? I want, I work: *Quiero trabajar.* I want, you work: *Quiero que trabajes.* Only when the person changes do you need *que* and the new ending. Today it follows *quiero que* and *necesito que*.
smallPrint: Teachers call this new shape the present subjunctive (*presente de subjuntivo*). Wanting is just the first door into it.

I want you to work with me.

Vale wants Tomás to stay.
Tomás wants Vale to stay.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *trabajas* or *trabajes* and type the whole sentence, to a friend: *Quiero que ___ conmigo.* (I want you to work with me.)
yourTurn.why: After *quiero que*, the verb takes the opposite vowel: *trabajes*.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *comer* or *que comas* and type the whole sentence: *Necesito ___ algo.* (I need to eat something.)
yourTurn.why: You need and you eat: same person, so the plain form.

yourTurn.prompt: Tell a friend: I need you to help me.
yourTurn.why: Two people, so *que* plus the new ending: *ayudes*.

yourTurn.prompt: Ask a friend: Do you want me to call you tomorrow?
yourTurn.why: You're the one calling, and for I the form is the same as for he or she: *llame*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: Vale wants Tomás to stay.
yourTurn.answer: Vale quiere que Tomás se quede.
yourTurn.why: Vale wants, Tomás stays: two people, so *que se quede*.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it negative: *Quiero que hables con Altamira.*
yourTurn.answer: No quiero que hables con Altamira.
yourTurn.why: The *no* goes before *quiero*; the rest stays the same.

yourTurn.prompt: Say it to a group (you all) instead of one friend: *Necesito que vengas temprano.*
Now you want a friend to do it, not you: *Quiero leer el contrato.* (I want you to read the contract.)
yourTurn.why: The reader changed, so add *que* and swap the vowel: *leas*.

pitfalls.why: Almost. Spanish can't copy I want you to; it says I want that you work: *quiero que trabajes*.
*Trabajas* states a fact. What you want someone to do takes the opposite vowel: *trabajes*.

pitfalls.wrong: Quiero que yo hable con él.
pitfalls.why: You want and you talk: same person, so no *que*, just *hablar*.
Build it like the command *venga*, from *vengo*: *vengas*.

personal: Think of someone in your life. Tell them one thing you really want them to do, starting with *Quiero que* or *Necesito que*.
